The comparatively low birth mass highlights a life-history trade-off where early developmental investment is deferred in favor of a later, more rapid growth trajectory during the nestling period. Sexual size dimorphism is pronounced in Strix uralensis, with adult females attaining a substantially greater ultimate wet weight compared to males. Females typically reach an asymptotic mass of 870 grams [Wwi = 870 grams], while males, the smaller sex, plateau at a significantly lower ultimate wet weight of 590 grams [Wwi = 590 grams]. This substantial difference, a female-to-male mass ratio of nearly 1.5, is among the highest recorded within the genus Strix and is likely driven by the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The larger body size in females also confers advantages in defending the nest and competing for high-quality territories. The initial mass of a newly laid egg, or initial wet weight, has been recorded at 49 grams [Ww0 = 49 grams], representing a considerable proportion of the female's own body mass. Such a large egg investment is a hallmark of species that produce small clutches, as it provides the developing embryo with a rich yolk reserve to sustain growth through the lengthy incubation period.

This conservative breeding strategy is closely tied to the fluctuating availability of their primary prey, small rodents such as voles, whose population cycles strongly influence clutch size and fledging success. In peak vole years, clutches of four eggs are occasionally recorded, whereas during population crashes, breeding may be entirely foregone. Such plasticity in reproductive effort highlights the species' adaptation to the unpredictable resource base of its taiga ecosystem.
